based on this idea that a success is someone who's been on television.
And what's more fascinating is this person isn't a failure at all.
She's a very successful corporate executive.
But she still had this agreement that she was a failure.
And she had all sorts of other ideas about what a failure was.
But as she looked behind that word, failure,
into all the different stories and images and beliefs about herself that were held there,
she could unravel all the little ones.
And pretty soon, failure became an empty word.
Empty in that it no longer had emotional charge to it.
I want to share another example.
And that one's come up multiple times where a woman believes she's a bad mother.
That term bad mother has all sorts of structures behind it about failing her children and what that means.
I was speaking with a woman.
She had a newborn baby, and she was working through feeding and changing and the crying and the sleep.
And sometimes she would pick up her new daughter, and she wouldn't stop crying.
and that she had a stepdaughter in the house
and stepdaughter would pick her up and just hold her and was wonderful with her.
And sometimes the young baby would stop crying.
And she would use little instances like that
to exaggerate, oh, I'm not doing it right,
into I'm failing as a mother to a more permanent title of I'm a bad mother.
The reason I bring this up is because it's not that uncommon.
Another client of mine, she concluded she was a bad mother because her son of about 10 years old
had told her an hour before he has a hockey game, and she didn't have a clean uniform for him.
She hadn't gotten to washing it yet.
So because he was going to go sweat in a uniform that wasn't clean, she concluded she was a bad mother.
But when you look at the details and you're more specific and precise in your word,
all you're saying is, okay, the laundry isn't done yet.
And he's going to go sweat in something that's already been sweated in.
No harm done.
But the correlations that we make, the exaggerations of what's implied in that,
can take us into a huge emotional reaction.
The easy way to break down a lot of that emotional charge
about huge agreements that we can have about one word
is to just look at the single word,
but then look at all the lines of thoughts and agreements that are behind it,
the whole structure that make that up.
My suggestion is that when you find a word that has emotional charge to it,
take that one word and dissect all the different meanings to it,
all the different agreements that radiate out from that one word
that you've accumulated over history.
You don't always know how you got these agreements,
and you don't have to figure that part out.
You just need to see which ones you're carrying around
and see if they make sense.
What you find out is, when they don't really make sense,
they start falling apart all by themselves.
What's extra interesting about the woman who felt like a failure
because she hadn't been on television,
is later, after she was dismantling the agreement,
she realized that she had been on television,
and yet she still hadn't broken the agreement about being a failure.
So it had nothing to do with reality,
but it had everything to do with her imagination and the perception of herself.

11 Core Beliefs Transcript
    pathwaytohappiness.com/courses/self-mastery-course-1/11-core-beliefs/11-core-beliefs-transcript
                                                                         May 11, 2019

Today’s lesson is what I call “implied” or “embedded” agreements. It has everything to
do with how we speak and assume, and the construct of our language. We’re going to
break it into three different sessions. The first one is about the implied and the
embedded agreements in the  statements . Then I’m going to break up what gets
implied and embedded in just  words , and I’m going to specifically talk about it in two
different ways.

Let’s just understand how big a word is in a way we dream our life. If I use the word
“betrayal”, that can create a whole image, scenario or even a whole couple years of our
life. Or if I use the word “romantic relationships”. Now we have all sorts of dreams and
ideas of all the relationships in our life, our hopes for what they would have been, our
hopes for what they will be. Just that one word takes us into some really big dreams
that can have lots of emotion. And there’s a whole structure of worlds just behind that
word. The same with the words like “ love ”, “ money ” or “ sex ”. We can go in so many
different directions about what our meaning or experience of those words are, and we
can have lots of different reactions, depending on the context. So, phrases and the way
we language things have a tendency to take us into huge dreams.

We are going to apply the way of approaching things that we learn in this exercise to
our agreements and our stories that have an emotional charge in them. If it’s just a story
where we talk with our friend, and there’s no emotional reaction, this exercise won’t
really help us much.

First thing I want to clarify is what’s the difference between a “discernment” and a
“judgment”, or what I sometimes call an “assessment” and a “judgment”. We have to
make honest assessments and evaluations of what’s working and what’s not working,
what is and isn’t so. But then we often skew it into a value or a judgment that have a
reaction that means something else. Let’s say, for instance, that I come home, and the
kitchen sink is full of dirty dishes, things haven’t been put away, and the kitchen is a
mess. What happens from there is the big question. The kitchen is not the way the
kitchen is supposed to be. But do I get upset when I look at it? Let’s say I was the one
that made the mess, and I look at the kitchen and go: “Wow, this kitchen is a mess,”
and I am just kind of noting the way that it is so. But what if I see the kitchen and go:
“Oh, wow, my (!) kitchen is a mess!!” – in this case there’re totally different tone and
attitude, and although I am not really saying any different words, I am drawing a
different conclusion. I’m saying: “My kitchen is a mess!” And I have implied in that
statement, just by the tone and attitude, that it shouldn’t look this way, that there’s a
whole other level of kitchen cleanness and order that should be present here. That’s
assumed, but is not spoken. Therefore it’s not looking the way that it should and there’s
a judgment there. And what’s more is that I’m kind of down on myself because my

                                                                                                                                         1/9

kitchen isn’t looking up to this unspoken standard. And I might even conclude: “Oh, my
kitchen is a mess… then I am a slob!” So, I’ve judged my kitchen and I’ve judged
myself while all that was said is what I call “an assessment”. It’s a fair assessment. The
kitchen is a mess. The part that isn’t true is that I’m a miserable human being for
making it such a mess and leaving it that way. See, I’ve implied that I am an unworthy
person because of how neat I am. I didn’t say any of it, but I’m having the emotional
reaction due to all those agreements. We could say that on the surface the facts are the
part I’m reacting to, but in the internal dialogue or what I say out loud about the kitchen,
there’s an unspoken story. And that story, based in facts, appears to be true.
Because the kitchen is indeed very untidy. But I’m not having a reaction to the facts. I’m
having a reaction to all my other implied agreements and assumptions of what it means
about myself as a person, and what it means about my self worth.

Let’s take another example. If I say to myself: “I’m late”, “I’m behind schedule,” – how
many things can we imply into that? How does it relate to our professional value or what
kind of person we are? How does that go to determine our emotional state? This is all is
done by agreement.

Also we can take comments that come from other people. And they can say:
“You’re late.” We can then interpret on our own that they’re being critical of us. They
may be or may not be. All that can go into the category of communication between
people, where we can ask questions so that we don’t have to make assumptions about
what they mean. But all that is for a different course. This lesson is about how you
interpret what they say. What else does that mean about you that you assume they
meant when they did or they didn’t? What do you assume or what do you believe about
that set of assumptions that isn’t spoken, but just implied, assumed, and you feel it
emotionally? That’s how you know it’s in there. This is where a lot of agreements hide
behind stories. Something even appearing factual like: “I am late”, “I am behind
schedule.” What does that mean about you and how does it affect you emotionally?

One of the biggest implied agreements that we make is that what we do or how well
we do it determines our self worth: the cleanness of the kitchen determines what
kind of person I am and the quality of the person I am; how well I perform at work, for
another people, as a mom; what kind of partner I am within a relationship. These are
things that we can imply meaning something about us. And not just that they mean
something about us, but more specifically that they determine what our self worth is.
And by what our self worth is I mean how lovable we are and how deserving of
being loved we are. The challenging part is to pull out the agreements from the stories
we tell that appear to be true, and see them as not being true. Let’s say we are at work
and something goes wrong, and it looks that we didn’t perform well. We so often apply
this value of our performance to our value as an employee, and then apply our value as
an employee to what our personal worth is. We don’t say these, don’t consciously imply
these, but subconsciously we make the implied agreements, and all of a sudden “I
didn’t do that very well,” or “I screwed that up,” becomes “I screwed that up!!” And it’s
just the difference in tone and attitude and it looks like what you’re saying is true. Yes,

                                                                                                                                  2/9

about that project – we screwed it up. But as a part of that package of “Oh, I screwed
that up,” we also have all those implied and embedded agreements that determine our
professional worth, our personal worth and our value, and that we’re screw up as a
person. We’re not saying it, but embedded in our tone and our attitude, it’s there. All
this is a part of that one package. And this is the way where we can so suddenly use
our words against ourselves. This can also be the case with what we tell other people.
We can say: “Hey, did you get this right?”, “Did you make this mistake?” And our
attitude and our tone can be a: “Did you make a mistake on this?” And it’s the tone, the
attitude, the emotional quality of that comment that we’re expressing. And while the
words say: “Hey, I’m just being neutral, I’m just talking about the performance,” we’re
also expressing our dissatisfaction about them professionally, out of which they might
conclude about themselves: “Oh, yeah I screwed that up!” And with that the implied and
embedded agreements go: “I am a screw up!” This is a subtle art of communication.
Cause we could even say it without any reference to the personal or professional value.
Just to have some question: “Hey, is this correct here what you’re presenting to me?
Cause that doesn’t seem that way to me.” And that’s a very neutral way to ask or
question what might be a mistake. But what do the other person’s Judge and Victim and
implied agreements determine from that? Who knows. You can only address your half
of these implied and embedded agreements, and you can communicate to other people
only as clearly as possible without an attitude of personal and professional worth.
They’re responsible for their half, and determining what it means about them
professionally, and what it means about them personally. What you can make great
strides in is being very clear to communicate that, so that at least the personalization of
it is minimized. And this is the same as we can do with what other people tell us. We
may feel like we’re attacked, but they may be very neutral and just talking about what
happened as far as our performance is concerned. And even though they may be
unhappy with our performance, that may mean nothing about us. All it depends on is on
each person’s implied assumptions, on how they embed their own agreements of
personal and professional worth into a situation. And these are not spoken, but they are
very much the paradigm of how we structure our emotional reactions. And as we look
at these kinds of stories and we pull them apart, we may find that just the simple
comments like: “Oh, I didn’t do that very well,” “Oh, it’s my fault that it didn’t turn out the
way it was supposed to,” may have a big emotional reaction.

Part two of this is looking at the specific words. There’re two kinds of words that
come up that are very good at hiding lies and self destructive agreements. One type of
words are words that are very general, very vague. Another type of words, where
agreements and lies hide and go against us, are words that are very absolute. For
example, absolute words that we need to be wary of are words like “never” and
“always”. I hear people in this work, in this process of undoing their agreements and
they win some, they loose some, they win some, they loose some, and they go up and
down on this ride of unraveling their emotional reaction, and at a certain point they feel
like: “I’m never going to make it.” My response to that is: “How long is “never”?” “Well
I’m not going to make it in my life time!” And my response to that “never”- being


                                                                                                                                 3/9

absolute, “life time” – being very vague. Because I ask: “How long is a life time?” “Well
somewhere between right now and next hundred years.” “OK, so what is it you know
you won’t be finished with those agreements?” And one of the reactions I might see is
they want to dismiss it and say: “Oh, you know what I meant.” Yeah, I know what they
meant. They meant they are struggling, it’s hopeless, and “I just want to give up.” That’s
what’s implied in: “Oh I feel like I’m never going to make it.” Because, based on their life
up until that point, maybe the six weeks or six years that they’ve been doing this work
of unraveling their agreements and their reactions, they haven’t made it during their “life
time”. Do they necessarily know what’s going to happen in the rest of their life time?
No, but they give the absolute statement: “I’m never going to make it”. And they give it
about something very vague, because I ask: “What is “it” that you’re not going to
make?”, “You know, “it”… to the other side,” “Well, what does that mean?”, “You know,
be happy in my life” (if I can get that precise an answer). But usually they are trapped in
such a vagueness that it’s hard for them to be so clear and simple about it. I say: “Ok,
then say it that way. But be honest and say what you mean and that’s: “I am never going
to be happy in my life”.” And when we see it that way, gosh, we don’t want to say that.
But we will say something vague and general like: “I won’t ever make it,” or “I won’t
ever get there.” Where is “there”? What is “there”?

Those are general terms, behind which we hide whole paradigms and dreams. We hide
the attitude of failure, of giving up. Then what we have to do is to avoid the words like
“it”, “there”, “never”, “always”, eliminate those very vague, general and absolute
words. Let’s be honest about what we’re feeling and speak specifically about it, so that
we can see the implied and embedded agreements in there and expose them for what
they are. Because “I feel like I’m never going to make it,” really means: “I have
agreements of hopelessness”, “I’ll never be happy in my life,” and “I just want to give
up.” At that point we can start look at what archetype character is that is speaking. And
now we start to stand outside that point of view. And if we’re more specific, we can say:
“At this moment it feels like I am in this dream where I will never be happy.”
Instead of saying the absolute “always”, what we need to do in this case is to be very
specific. Shift the words so that we can say: “In this moment I feel that I won’t make
it in my life to being really happy… Do I always feel this way? No. Right now I feel
this way.” Now we’ve gone from the absolute to something very specific. We’re close to
the truth and we don’t have this big weight of “I’ll never going to make it”. We’re being
more specific saying: “At this moment it feels like it’s unattainable”. Now it’s at least
possibly attainable, cause it doesn’t fall into the category of “never” and we’re saying,
“This is the point of view I am in right now.” Then the possibility gets a little bigger.
These are the problems we get into, when we say about our relationships struggles: “I’ll
always be alone.” We get that very sabotaging, life ending voice in our head once in a
while. Is it telling the truth about the totality of our life or is it really just expressing what
we’re feeling in this moment? Obviously it’s expressing what we’re feeling in this
moment. But if we really believe those words as vague as they are, we start to feel like
our whole life will be like that. And then, why to get up in the morning? But if we can
recognize more specifically, without the vagueness and generalities, without the


                                                                                                                                  4/9

absolute, that “In this moment, I’m in the point of view where things appear like I won’t
be happy in my life,” then we can start to dismantle and say: “OK, do I always feel like
this? No, I do not always feel like this!” And now this emotion isn’t as overwhelming. We
haven’t amplified this situation to: “I’ll always be that way.” That, which was an absolute,
which we were convincing ourselves of for the future of our life, we turned around and
saw as something that wasn’t true in the past. And if that wasn’t true in the past, how do
we know it’s going to be true in the future?

The hard part is in catching the statement. Catching the “its”, “there”, “always”, “never”.
Those are the hard words to catch. To hear what’s coming off our mind, to hear the
thoughts passing through our head and to question them and say: “What does that
really mean?” We have a chance to start putting doubt into our agreements by
breaking them down to something smaller.

Doubt is a very powerful force. Doubt can knock us off our track in life. If we doubt what
we’re doing or we doubt the outcome, then we give up, let it fall apart. What if we start
to doubt these self sabotaging agreements? To look at them and say: “Is that really
true? Maybe it’s not true? Maybe if my kitchen is a mess, I am not a miserable person?”
Why not doubt the self sabotaging agreements? Why not put doubt in our favor? It’s
kind of fun. All we have to do is ask ourselves: “Is that really true?”, and look at the
words behind it. Pull apart the ones that are vague and general so that we can see what
we are really saying and the agreements behind what we are really saying and start to
go: “Ok, are those little agreements really true? Is my self worth based on how I
perform at the office? Is my self worth based on what this one person of the 5 billion
people on the planet thinks about me? Why?” This is starting to use doubt as a tool to
break apart all those lies. We used doubt to sabotage a great dream of love in our life
and self worth. Why not to use doubt to sabotage and destroy the self doubt and
unworthiness? It could be fun. What makes one story true and not the other? Why not
to challenge all of them and see what stands up to scrutiny?

The reason that the really sabotaging, self destructive and the most depressing stories
appear true is because they are usually wrapped up with vague or very absolute words
like “always”, “never”, “nobody”, “somebody”, “everybody”. Those got to go. They
just have to go. Be more specific about what you say and look at the agreements that
are implied and embedded underneath those things you say. Because when you pull
out the details of the other agreements you see that they don’t make sense and they
just start falling apart. Why do my self worth, the whole value of my life depend upon
what I did at work this one week or what this person has to say about it? Does that
determine my self worth for my life? All of a sudden it starts to not make sense. And a
doubt comes in and we don’t give that opinion that much power. And we start to see
that there’s a lot more to us than that one opinion, and that our performance in one
week does not determine our professional value, our professional value does not
determine our personal worth, and it certainly does not determine how much we can
love and be happy in our life. But those are all the chain of agreements that are implied
when we have a reaction to something. Scrutinizing our attitude and our emotional

                                                                                                                                   5/9

reactions to different comments – that’s where we will find the agreements. Not in
the words, cause the words look like the facts. They look like it’s true, like we screwed
that up. OK, we screwed that up, but that doesn’t mean that we are screwed up. All it
means is that we are learning, growing, and becoming better at what we do by growing
from the mistakes that we make. The same way the child learns to walk by falling down
and learning what doesn’t work. That’s how we get better at doing what does work.

I’ll give you another sequence that becomes an exaggeration. It’s one of the most
powerful sequences that I see people make in terms of implied agreements. It’s a very
ironic thing because expressing our words, creating a dream of ourselves as a huge
failure, isn’t a very powerful act. Some times we do this kind of projection in a way that
we make ourselves powerless. Here’s the example: we go and try to change something
like taking things personally. We don’t get it the first or the second time. We keep going,
but we make the assessment of our self of “I’m not getting this”. We can say, “I’m not
getting it” or we can say, “I (!) am not getting it,” – a very different set of agreements. In
the latter we have the assessment of the past and we picture ourselves as a failure.
Then we exaggerate it to the future and then we add to this the idea that: “If we’re a
failure and what we have tried to change hasn’t changed, then we cannot change
it any longer,“ “I’ve tried to not take it personally but I can’t.” Now we imply the
agreement that we have been powerless to change ourselves, and we project into the
future that we are powerless to change ourselves. That’s the difference from going from
“I haven’t gotten this yet” to “I’m not getting this” to “I (!) am not getting this!” That kind
of agreement, where we try to change and we fall into the implied agreement that “we
can’t” and that “we won’t” in the future time, is agreeing to this idea that we’re powerless
to change our self. Then next iteration after that exaggeration becomes: “Well if I’m
powerless to change myself, and I can’t stop these habits, why should I even
try?” Now we’ve gone from “I’m failing” to “Don’t bother.” And if we go to “Don’t
bother,” now we’re in the emotion of despair, and then we look at our life forward and
see that we don’t have the power to change ourselves, and therefore don’t have the
power to change anything, and then we end up in hopelessness. And from
hopelessness we go easily to depression. So we’ve gone from failure to the
exaggeration of the future failure, to the exaggeration of “I am a failure. I’ve tried to
change and I can’t. Therefore I’m powerless to change.” And if we agree we’re
powerless, we have the emotion of despair, we give up and there’s a depression. That
kind of slow iteration of change and stacking up of agreements started as something
that’s based in fact like “I tried to make this change and I couldn’t”. It started as
something that was an actual assessment without judgment. But you see, we start
exaggerating into present time, future time, what it means about us. Every step along
the way is one more slight iteration and agreement change and exaggeration based on
the previous one. And none of them stand out as really gaping lies. Because it’s hardly
a shift from one to the other, but when you stack up several agreements in a row that at
each there are slight shifts and exaggeration of the previous one, you see how you talk
yourself into hopelessness, despair and depression. And this is a very powerful act.
This is an extraordinary act of power for us to use our word as a Magician. To create


                                                                                                                                6/9

that whole structure and image of ourselves that we can push our emotional body and
get that kind of result. Our nature is to be expressive. This is our natural state. But it’s
not our normal state in our life, because most people are way down with heavy
agreements. But it is our natural state and it takes a phenomenal act of power to make
ourselves convinced that we’re powerless and to not take action. That’s the great irony
here. Then, what I see is someone who has incredible amount of power and is using it
to convince themselves, through the structure of these agreements they are committed
to, that they are not powerful and because they are so powerful, they are able to
accomplish it. To me that’s an extraordinary feat of a great magician, granted they don’t
know what they are doing with their magic. But you can’t tell me they are not powerful.

All of this is based in the impeccability of our word. All the interpretations we make, the
implied and the embedded agreements, the way we picture ourselves, the scenarios we
picture of ourselves in the future. These are our own expressions of our word. Not just
the words that come out of our mouth or that we think, but in how we create and
express the whole picture of ourselves in the dream of our imagination. So many
distortions of the ways we use our word to go against ourselves exist there, and they
are never spoken, but they are expressed.

So, your mission, should you choose to accept it, is to notice the places where you
have an emotional reaction, either to what you say or what you think, or to what
someone else has said, but that you interpret in a way that gives you an emotional
reaction from there. And in those phrases, those words, those experiences where you
have an emotional reaction, you need to look for what agreements are behind the story,
what agreements are implied. And specifically look for words that are very vague,
general and absolute. And as a writing exercise you’re going to write about: 1) What
happened in a short hand version – the words that came out of your mouth; 2) Then
you’re going to write the second version that include all the implied and the embedded
agreements in there, and what all those words really meant in terms of the agreements
of our belief system. Write down how they came out so that you can see how you
created your emotional reaction; 3) And then you use doubt. Use doubt in your favor
this time. Instead of doubting yourself, you’re going to use doubt on those agreements
and those stories and ask yourself: “Is that story really true? Do I really know what
the future’s going to be like?” Getting to total hopelessness and despair is just a few
agreements away from telling a fact, and getting out of hopelessness and despair is just
revealing those agreements to yourself and doubting. Just wondering: “Is there
another way this could be? Is this really the truth of the way it is?” You don’t have
to break all the agreements. All you have to do is to start doubting them. And that doubt
is so powerful that those agreements start to fall apart all by themselves. And they do it
simply because you’re no longer holding them up. 4) And then the third version – you
write out what you really want to say that is an honest assessment, without the
exaggeration, without the implied and imbedded agreements, so that you speak
specifically and honestly about “what is”, without distorting it with projections in your
mind.


                                                                                                                                     7/9

As you practice this you may find writing it out isn’t necessarily always handy. But I
suggest you write this out, so that it’s clear what happened in the first round, all the
detailed agreements that were in there and how we got the emotional reaction we did,
and then the clarification expression, which is really how we want to practice speaking.
Writing it down will help keep all this straight. Doing it in your head can often take you
for another spin ride. That’s why writing it down will help for the clarity. After you’ve
been writing it down for a while something pops up in your mind and your catch it in the
moment and you can see all the agreements behind it and dissolve the emotional
reaction. That’s when you can let go of the writing that process.

As we investigate these implied and embedded agreements, we can find that there can
be huge structures of beliefs and emotional charge behind a single word. And the
types of words that usually have the greatest emotional charge have to do with
ourselves and, specifically, with the descriptive terms about ourselves. We can have a
lot of emotional charge about the words like “loyalty”, depending on who it’s applied to,
“responsibility”, “heart break” or “heartbroken”. If we describe ourselves as
“heartbroken”, it usually has a strong emotional charge.

Lets take a word like “failure”. Failure can have so many references and particularly
emotional links to meaning in our history. We can go back and see we made an
agreement in the fifth grade about what kind of person we were at math or spelling, and
we haven’t yet gone back to dissolve it. We may have put other agreements on top of it
though: about how smart we are and about how successful and capable we are. But it
doesn’t mean we’ve dissolved this other one that’s lying underneath. A client of mine
was working through these implied and embedded agreements and specifically on the
word “failure”. And she was taking a word and brainstorming about everything that
came to mind about the word “failure”, and about what it meant. And she was doing it
because she had a belief she was a failure. She was trying to figure out what it was.
She didn’t know exactly why she was a failure. She just felt at times that she was. By
doing this she also had to take apart a word “success”. Cause it’s the duality structure
of failure and you have to have a success to compare it to. One defines the other. This
is why we band all these words, because we’re much more than something that could
be divided in “either-or”. What she realized was that she was a failure because success
meant that she had to appear on a national television. And she’s like: “Why do I need
that for success?” – she couldn’t figure it out. Well, she didn’t have to. She just realized
it wasn’t true. It was very shocking for her to realize all this. And what’s more
fascinating is that this person isn’t a failure at all, but a very successful corporate
executive. And she had all sorts of other ideas about what a “failure” was. But as she
looked behind that word “failure” into all the different stories and images and beliefs
about herself that were held there, she could unravel all the little ones. And pretty soon
“failure” became an empty word. Empty in that it no longer had an emotional charge to
it.





                                                                                                                               8/9

Another example that comes out multiple times is when woman believes she’s a bad
mother. And that term “bad mother” has all sorts of structures behind it about failing her
children and what that means. I was speaking with a woman who had that problem. And
another one as well. They concluded they were bad mothers because of some small
accidents. The correlations that we make, the exaggerations of what’s implied in those
agreements about those small accidents can take us into a huge emotional reaction.
The easy way to break down a lot of that emotional charge about huge agreements that
we can have about one word, is to first just look at the single word, but then, and this is
the most important, to look at all the lines of thoughts and agreements that are behind
it, to the whole structure that made that up.

My suggestion is that when you find a word that has emotional charge to it, take that
one word and dissect all the different meanings of it, all the different agreements that
radiate out from that one word that you’ve accumulated over history. You don’t always
know how you got these agreements and you don’t have to figure that part out. You just
need to see which ones you’re carrying around and see if they make sense. What you’ll
find out is that when they don’t really make sense they start falling apart all by
themselves.

What’s extra interesting about the woman who felt like a failure because she hadn’t
been on television, is later she actually realized that she had been on television, and
yet she still hadn’t broken the agreement about being a failure. So, it had nothing to do
with reality, but everything to do with her imagination and with her perception of herself.





                                                                                                                                9/9

                                                                         May 10, 2019



11 Core Beliefs

We’re moving all courses to the new Self Mastery Community

Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/i5FZwgR5PjE

Summary of practice

1. Listen to the Core Beliefs lesson audio
You may want to listen multiple times. You will find that I often refer to these beliefs as
Embedded, or Implied, or Hidden Agreements. They are all the same.

2. Go through the writings of what your characters have said and thought.Look
for the gaps in logic, the false assumptions, and beliefs that are implied in what they
say. This will give you a way to crack apart a thought that appears true, and see it as
false.

3. Feel free to use a lot of paper. You might find yourself taking one statement from a
character and writing a page or pages about all the thoughts, emotions, and underlying
beliefs behind it.

Some notes

There are many ways to diagram out what the mind is doing through these characters.
Myself, and my clients have found it extremely helpful to mind-map or diagram out the
structure of these beliefs. You can do it different ways. My method generally looks like
a chart. Others use more of a mind-map. You can even get mind-map apps for your
phone or computer if you wish to sort through beliefs that way.

We embed many agreements and beliefs into just a few words. The words become
symbols for entire dreams and patterns of beliefs. We say the words but our mind
implies all sorts of other meanings into it from related beliefs.

Let’s take the example of trying to stop an emotional reaction. We fail at our first
attempt and our second attempt. We say the words, “I can’t do this.” Truthfully the real

                                                                                                                                           1/5

meaning is, “I wasn’t able to stop it this time.”
But when we use the short hand general description, “I can’t do this,” we invoke
memories and dreams of failing in the past. This brings in all the agreements of the
past experiences where we said, “I can’t do this.” The words are a trigger for other
agreements that we have, but don’t apply to the current situation. We project all these
meanings into the current situation and feel the emotion of our projection. We
exaggerate and lie with our meanings about the future. Embedded in the feeling and
attitude is “I will never be able to do this.” The emotion then becomes hopelessness.
Then we feel the emotion of our embedded and implied lies. To avoid this we refrain
from general terms, and vague descriptions and practice speaking specifically about
what is happening.

One layout might look like this:

                      Story and Imbedded     Emotion
                   Agreements

 Victim                           I can’t do this              Feeling of failure

 Meaning                        I failed at this              Feeling worse

 Which means                I am a failure at this        Feeling even worse

 Added meaning from    I was a failure in the past   Larger feeling of failure
 memory

 Exaggerated                  I fail at everything        More

 Projected                       I will fail in the future      More
 exaggeration

 Amplified and made      I will always be a failure   And More emotion of failure and
 personal                                   overwhelmed

 In the meaning of words, and the meaning of phrases are beliefs and whole new
stories with other characters. It has been the development of your Hunter/Observer
characters thus far that will help you to see through what these thoughts “say” on the
surface, and perceive what the beliefs are in the meaning.
Often you will feel the meaning of a statement in the emotion rather than the words.
The words might be factually true, but the embedded beliefs give you a different feeling.
The emotion tells you more about what beliefs are buried in the meaning of those
words.

Resistance to change
                                                                                                                                    2/5

This is hard….. or so one of the characters said. And this would be a 1/2 Truth. The
thing about a 1/2 Truth is that is is also 1/2 Lie. It’s really valuable to see the lie and not
believe that part. If you are half in a lie and half in a Truth then you don’t go anywhere.

The half Truth part is that this is work. It is an effort to dissect your beliefs, release the
emotions, move your attention and point of view. Yes that is work. It is work to lift these
beliefs off your mind and free your awareness.

The half lie that it leaves out is that it doesn’t tell you how hard life is if you avoid this
work. If you don’t make these efforts that lead to these changes, what happens? What
thoughts, beliefs, and emotions do you continue to have? What behaviors do your
characters continue to push you to do? How hard is your life when you live under the
rule of your characters afraid to make changes to them?

To me, living under the berating of the Judge, or the fear of the Victim, the constant
efforts of the Pleaser to make others happy, or the Hero to try and be good enough to
satisfy other people’s Judge, is living in insanity in my own mind. That is a much harder
life. This work is hard, that is true. But not doing this work is also hard, and includes
miserable suffering with no way out.

It is work to change these beliefs, however I preferred this to surrendering to these
characters I had previously created.

I didn’t know if I would ever get free from all of them, but I knew I had to try. I would fail
many times. But any kind of progress made my life better. Even if I didn’t make it all the
way, a happier life was better than giving up.

Common questions

How to organize all this information?
See these articles for examples of taking an inventory of beliefs. It includes the
characters and emotions so you can see it all at once.

What if you see those beliefs as true?
Often beliefs are 1/2 True. They can appear true from the point of view of a character.
However, from a skeptic, they don’t appear true, or even false. They appear as
concepts and we are skeptical as to whether they are true or not. We are undecided.

So in this process, you may not get to seeing the statement as false right away. But, if
you can see it in a way that,,,, hmmm…. it might not be true. Then that’s progress.

Then the next step, is to question it in different ways.

Is it always true?





                                                                                                                                    3/5

If it is a belief about your self, Was this true when I was 6 weeks old? At what point in
my life did this belief begin to become true? If it wasn’t true when I was born, then it
was a believe I acquired.

If the story is, “I’m not good enough”, or “I’m a terrible person.” then it wasn’t true when
you were born. It wasn’t true the first year of your life. Then, something happened, and
it started to seem, or feel true after that. Who were you before you acquired this belief?

If you didn’t feel that same emotion, would the belief still appear true?

How much does the emotion affect the belief?
Emotion entirely affects the belief. In a very subjective way, most beliefs only appear
true because they feel true.

These emotions go with the judgments, and victim beliefs about our selves. If we didn’t
feel the unworthiness, shame, or guilt, then we could laugh off the concepts of the
stories very easily.

For this reason, it is helpful to keep up the releasing emotions exercise.

What if you intellectually know a belief is a lie, but you still believe it?
This is progress. Very often we can see with our intellect, or observer, that a belief is a
lie, or false. Yet, we know the feeling. The feeling is that we still believe it.

This is because over years you have unconsciously invested your personal power of
faith into that belief, and the underlying assumptions or embedded beliefs that support
it.

This faith resides in the concept still and keeps the belief empowered as a kind of living
force in your mind. This faith can come out over time through repetitions of skepticism.
It can also empty out very fast with a strong experience of something that counters it.
This usually takes a strong emotional experience. Even then, it may not completely
burst the original belief.

For a while you might have both beliefs. They may be in opposition to each other. This
is a good time to see it as characters. One character point of view sees the second as
false. But the second character is in a completely different belief bubble and perceives
the first character as false.

This kind of cognitive dissonance is actually a good, although uncomfortable. Staying
present with the dissonance feeling is a good process to stay with. The more you are
aware of this dissonance, the more you can see the virtual structures of your mind, and
the more you will move into Consciousness about what the mind does.

That feeling of dissonance is your consciousness seeing a concept that it believes is
true, but knows it isn’t true. It’s like looking at two conflicting realities. Yet, your
awareness knows which one is false. The more you can stay in this awareness, will

                                                                                                                                    4/5

benefit you. It is a state where your unconscious mind is learning to break from a
previously held version of what it thought was reality, and embrace a different version of
“reality.”

Supporting videos

Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/EzQSZhOnmxY

Mind Map Belief Inventory of Jealousy

You can use pictures and arrows to make your inventory. It doesn’t need to be a chart
or excel sheet. Symbols or images can be very powerful and in some ways more
memorable for your awareness.

Watch Video At: https://youtu.be/1U1zmGtYTxU

Understanding Belief Systems

You may have seen this before. If it has been a couple months, your insights from the
course and practices will allow you to hear it completely differently now.





                                                                                                                                     5/5

Core Belief Inventory: Anger

   pathwaytohappiness.com/blog/core-belief-inventory-anger

                                                                             December 12, 2018

Last Updated on August 28, 2019

The process of developing self mastery requires that we be completely honest with our
self. One of the tools to assist in this complete honesty is the core belief inventory. By
making an inventory you can break through the layers of denial, ego, image projection,
and false beliefs. In this way we have an opportunity to be more authentic.

Some people think that you will unravel your beliefs by writing down the thoughts in
your head. If you do that you will be missing many of the underlying beliefs below those
thoughts. There’s a more effective way. To give you an idea of what is involved in a core
belief inventory I’ve charted out an example below.

If you are hoping to change an emotional reaction it can be difficult. Either it is too big
to stop, and you get carried away, or you don’t even know where to start. In the example
I break down an emotional reaction into smaller and smaller pieces. In this thin slicing
approach you are able to see that an emotional reaction of anger is actually formed and
sustained by several different beliefs, and several different points of view. One of the
easy ways to change an emotional reaction like anger is to break it down into smaller
manageable pieces.

One of the skills you learn in the Self Mastery program is how to identify and change
these dynamics your self. Below is an example inventory from one of my clients that
helped build his awareness of all the contributing elements and change his emotional
reactions

Example: Feeling Angry and Frustrated With Your Boss

Feeling frustrated and angry at work is way too common. A common source of
frustration and anger is our relationship with our boss. I’ll share with you about Mike
who felt frustrated and even angry at the lack of recognition for his efforts at work.
What is important about this story is what Mike’s beliefs were in connection with the
story. The beliefs in Mike’s mind have as much or more to do with his frustration as his
boss. But we usually don’t look at those beliefs. We are usually too busy noticing what
our boss is doing or not doing to catch what the mind is up to. In Mikes case he was
unaware of the beliefs behind is thoughts. When he took the time to take an inventory of
his beliefs he saw a way of eliminating the frustration he was having with his boss.

Mike’s original understanding of what caused his frustration





                                                                                                                                   1/5

Mike doesn’t feel valued by his boss. She (the boss) doesn’t appreciate what he has to
contribute. At times she doesn’t even want to hear his ideas. He feels frustrated and
even gets angry at his boss for closing the door on what he is passionate about.

If Mike doesn’t want to feel frustrated and angry any more what can
he do?

Some people might advise that he attempt to open the lines of communication with her.
Others might tell Mike to let it go, don’t make such a big deal about it, or get another job
if it really bothers him.

He has tried to have a discussion with his boss about the issue but she shrugs it off. She
doesn’t feel it is a problem and wants Mike to get on with his work. She is not as
interested in Mike’s ideas as with getting the job done the way she wants it done.

Opening up lines of communication with someone in order to clear the air is a good
idea. But if you aren’t aware of different aspects of your own personality then you may
be headed into the conversation blind. To see the rest of the picture Mike might be
better served by understanding how his belief system affects his emotions.

When Mike shared this situation he was aware that he had a role in the emotional
dynamic, but didn’t know what part was his responsibility. He also didn’t know what
was getting his emotions stirred up. There were various aspects of his personality that
were at play that he hadn’t identified. I refer to these aspects as archetype characters.
Using archetype characters becomes a helpful way to break out the subtle differences
between emotions like anger and frustration.

Understanding the Whole Picture of what the Mind is Doing

Mike shared the other stories that were going on in his mind. They weave beliefs
together to form a string of emotional reactions that I outline below.

    1. She (the boss) is not open to new ideas.
   2. The organization would be better off if she were more open and implement some
      of his ideas.
   3. She wants to maintain control
   4. She should recognize my value and what I have to contribute.

It didn’t take long for Mike to look at these comments and figure out it was his inner
judge running with these stories.

Some other thoughts and feelings Mike had in his mind

    1. Mike also noticed he felt sad just before he felt angry about the lack of recognition.
   2. Mike felt that he could do her job better than her.




                                                                                                                                   2/5

3. Mike had become aware that his anger was pushing up ideas of defiance and
      rebellion. He wanted to sabotage the boss’s efforts and prove she was doing things
     wrong. These weren’t thoughts he wanted to have.

Fortunately Mike had enough awareness to observe the different attitudes and emotions
in this dynamic and so this only took a few minutes. With that we laid out the matrix of
beliefs that were at the core of his emotional reactions. It looked like this.


 Archetype  Storyline and / or Behavior                 Emotion
 Character

 Princess    Ideal of how Mike should be treated by his boss. This   Pride, self
              included recognition to the degree that his ideas had   worth, but also
               to be implemented.                                          self importance
                                                        and ego

 Victim      Boss wasn’t recognizing Mike according to hidden     Hurt, sad,
                 criteria of expectations. Mike believed he was being     feeling of
              mistreated relative to this criteria.                   unworthiness

 Victim    My personal value is based on my contributions. This  Disempowering
             paradigm isn’t spoken but is hidden in the reaction.

 Victim     Mike held his boss responsible for his hurt and        Powerlessness
              sadness (blame). This victim interpretation gave him
             a feeling that she had power over his emotions.

 Authentic   I want to change this feeling.                       Emotional
 Desire                                                                Integrity

 Victim       “I want to change this situation and emotion but I      Frustration,
 (distorts      can’t.” Having given power over his emotion to his    and feeling
 the          boss creates the paradigm that he can’t change his     trapped
 authentic   own emotions.
 desire)

 Judge      The feeling of powerlessness added to his story that    Sense of being
              she was controlling.                                     right about her.

 Judge      She hurt him and therefore should be punished.       Righteous

 Judge      The boss shouldn’t be so controlling and instead       Feeling of
              should be more open to ideas.                       being right (self
                                                               importance)

 Judge      She is a poor boss and is not doing a good job.         Righteous

 This series of judgments is a reaction to the disempowering beliefs of the victim
 character. It is a way compensate by building himself up and feeling better
 emotionally. The image of himself on the moral high ground is closer to authenticity
 but falsely based. It only supports the rationalizations for his anger.

                                                                                                                                   3/5

Judge      “Because I am right and she is wrong I have the       Righteous and
             moral high ground here. Punishment is now          moral
               authorized.”

 Rebel       “I’m going to punish her by directing my anger at     Anger
                her.”

 Rebel       “I’m going to sabotage her projects to prove I’m right.  Sense of
              This retribution will be justice.”                       defiance and
                                                                            justice about it

Sometimes people give up the fight to be heard and get their ideas across. They let go of
their passion, but keep the sense of powerlessness from the victim’s archetype. This is a
set up to feed stories of judgment and anger later. They don’t feel frustrated, but they
aren’t happy and fulfilled either.

When you inventory and change the specific problem beliefs you can let go of what
upsets you while continuing to be inspired and engaged by the aspects of work you
enjoy. In Mike’s case he can shift the expectations of his boss without throwing in the
towel about other aspects of his job.

Trying to solve the problem without Self Awareness

Consider the scenario of Mike not being aware of how his belief system was interpreting
his boss’s behavior. Consider that he is not aware of how the archetypes of his
personality are affecting his attitude and emotions. If Mike were to seek an open
communication dialogue with his boss how would it go? He would likely and
unknowingly bring attitudes of judgment, victimization, princess expectations, and
rebellion to the conversation. Mike would probably feel “right” according to his belief
system and archetypes, but that wouldn’t make for a healthy constructive dialogue.

Looking inward and taking responsibility for our half of the emotional reaction is an
uncommon approach. However it is also the empowering one. If we look outwards and
point the finger at someone else we are claiming to be powerless over what is happening
inside ourselves. Being aware that our happiness and emotions are a product of our
beliefs puts the capacity for change in our own hands.

If you take careful notice of the chain reaction of stories and emotions you will see that
the first reaction was to his boss. From then on Mike was basically reacting to his the
interpretations in his mind and the emotions he felt. The belief system and voices in his
head was reacting to itself.

As self awareness grows you gain more dominion over the core beliefs in your mind and
the characters of your personality. Awareness and responsibility allow you to dispense
with unpleasant emotional reactions by choosing how you interpret events and what
you will believe. Dominion over your beliefs allows you to create happiness for yourself
in all your relationships.
                                                                                                                                   4/5

In the Self Mastery Course I walk you through the steps so that you can create an
inventory of the thoughts and small beliefs behind an emotional issue. By breaking the
situation down into the smaller pieces you gain more awareness and reactions become
easier to change.

Note

This isn’t the sum total of what is going on in Mike’s belief system. It is what we worked
out in about 10 minutes and gave him plenty to work with for a while. There are more
agreements embedded within the stories that came out later.





                                                                                                                                   5/5

Core Beliefs About Your Body

   pathwaytohappiness.com/blog/core-beliefs-body

                                                                              December 7, 2006

Last Updated on September 16, 2019

How do beliefs about food and our body affect our emotions?

I’ll use one woman’s story about her relationship with her body to illustrate the affect
beliefs in the mind can have. Shelly wanted to lose weight but it was a struggle to
exercise and eat healthy food. It seemed the body didn’t behave as it should and
rebelled against her wishes.

She had never been very athletic but had worked hard in the past to exercise, lose
weight, and get her body into good shape. The problem was that her body didn’t want to
stay there. If she didn’t stay on top of the issue her body would put on pounds again.
Shelly was tired of the struggle to win the short term battles only to lose the war over
her weight.

Shelly described her relationship with her body as that of a misbehaving child. The body
didn’t want to obey her wishes. The hard work to get her body into shape was like
punishment that was needed to get a child to behave.

After years of the same routine with her body without lasting progress, she was willing
to adopt a new point of view. It only makes sense that if we want a different result we
will have to take a different approach.

Shelly has Two Children

Let’s start by considering that Shelly has two misbehaved children. She has a body that
doesn’t follow the rules and she also has a mind that is misbehaving. It spurts out
opinions, judgments, and punishments about the body in an uncontrolled and
sometimes abusive manner. It is also the mind that is making the rules for the body. The
frustration and disappointment for the body isn’t from Shelly, it is from the character
voices in her head. It is the beliefs and stories of her mind that emotionally abuse her
body.

It is easy to realize that our thoughts are not our own. A big clue is if we attempt to turn
off our thoughts and we can’t. If they were our thoughts they would stop when we want
them to. Since they don’t turn off we can consider them as part of our mind that has
taken on a life of its own. It is our mind that has become like a misbehaved child that
runs amuck making a mess in our head and with our emotions.

To help become aware of the different stories, beliefs, and emotions, I like to lay them
out in an orderly table. A first cut at Shelly’s character voices and dialogue from her
mind looked like this.
                                                                                                                                   1/4

Voice in
   her                                                   Result on
  Head                  Story or Belief                 Emotions

  Judge   Body image in the mind. This is what my body      Hope
            should look like.

  Judge  My body doesn’t look like it should.                   Right, truthful
            (based on the body image above this looks like a
              truthful statement)

  Victim    “I” don’t look like I should.  Self rejection.            Sadness, feeling
            Almost the same statement but comes from a         not good enough.
              different part of our mind that agrees with the judge.

Shelly has a strong type A personality that is success oriented. She outlines tasks and
knocks them out with efficiency. This helps her feel like a successful winner. This is the
way her belief system structures criteria for allowing her to express love for herself, or
withhold love for herself. These criteria in the mind are the gate keepers for her
emotional happiness. Her mind applies the same program to her body image as she
does to a job at work. However this might not be the most helpful approach to raising
children, and that includes our body and mind. Her mind set the goal for her body to be
a size 8.

Because of the preceding agreed to beliefs about her body, Shelly’s belief system
concludes some things about herself.


   Voice        Story or Belief              Resulting Emotion

 Authentic   I want a healthy and fit      Emotional integrity
   Desire    body.

  Judge’s     If I am a size 8 I will fit my   Basis for success.
  Criteria   image of success.

   Hero      I need to be a size 8 in       Hope, goal, prize that determines self
              order to succeed.            worth.

   Judge    The body is not yet a size 8.   Righteous authority figure.

  Victim     I am failure for not             I am a failure, loser, not good enough,
              reaching my goal.            sad, depressed.

   Judge    Blames the body for the      Hates the body for creating the feeling of
                 failure.                     being not good enough.

    Body size is the means by which her belief system determines her worth. Happiness is
    now dependent on a number sewn into the label on an article of clothing. This can create
     an added feeling of powerlessness over her emotional happiness.

                                                                                                                                   2/4

Shelly has at the core of the story a purely authentic desire for her body to be healthy
and fit. The problem is that her mind has taken that desire and given winning and
losing criteria to it by which she judges herself. These stories and beliefs in the mind are
the source of her unhappiness, not her body.

Needless to say it isn’t a fun scenario for Shelly. Her mind set up criteria for her body
and then judged and rejected her body for not meeting the mind’s criteria. The child-
like mind is abusing the body with its comments and Shelly is experiencing the
emotional punishment from the active voices in her head. It isn’t not only the physical
body that ends up being punished. Shelly’s emotional body is being abused by the mind.
It is helpful to realize that neither the physical body or the emotional body did anything
wrong to deserve the punishment.

From the mind’s point of view feeling better emotionally requires that the body become
a certain size. Shelly’s belief system only authorizes the expression of love for the body
when the criterion of size 8 is met. If her body doesn’t change the belief system
considers Shelly a failure.

Chances for success with this mindset are bleak when our emotions are sabotaged in
this way. For starters Shelly’s mind develops frustration and hate at her body for
keeping her from being happy. The lack of expressing love facilitates unhappiness and
depression. These emotions create a mindset that drives her to eat unhealthy food and
avoid working out at the gym. When the emotionally abusive mind is in charge of child
raising the body in this way, things are headed in a downward spiral.

The challenge in realizing these dynamics of the mind is to shift her point of view out of
the internal dialogue far enough to see the mind as having a life of its own. It gives
opinions, stories, judgments, and criticisms like a misbehaved child. Shifting her point
of view far enough is what will keep her from judging herself for what the mind is doing.

If we look at our mind as being separate from us we can begin to see nonsensical
elements here. The mind sets up the goals, plans the “fix it” agendas, makes the
decisions about food and exercise, and then takes no responsibility for the results.
Instead it dishes out the criticisms and punishments about the body and doesn’t
acknowledge itself as ring leader or even party to the process. This is the kind of
nonsensical things belief systems do when they are allowed to operate without self
awareness.

Exercise Your Mind to Make It Healthy

What might happen if Shelly exercised her mind? Or should I say exorcised her mind.
How could Shelly feel emotionally if she got her mind settled down and it stopped
emotionally abusing her and her body? We could think of this as getting her mind to act
like an adult instead of the emotionally abusive and misbehaved child.

If Shelly eliminated some of the beliefs that kept her from loving and appreciating her
body her emotions would change. She could stop letting her mind treat her body like a
                                                                                                                                   3/4

misbehaved child that needed to be punished.

Shelly could then start to treat her body with love, and respect, just like children need to
be treated. Just like children, our bodies respond and behave better when treated with
love and respect than with abuse. As Shelly loves her body more she will naturally take
good care of it. She would want to feed it only healthy foods. She would also want her
body to get out and feel the euphoria of good exercise.

If we are to have a healthy relationship with our body we will also have to work on the
relationship we have with our mind, and how the mind treats our body. Consider
engaging in some emotionally healthy exercises for your mind and your belief system.





                                                                                                                                   4/4

Feeling Deprived
   pathwaytohappiness.com/blog/feeling-deprived
                                                                           December 15, 2018

Last Updated on August 26, 2019

Beliefs about Food, Eating and Feeling Deprived When Dieting
A common story people face when changing eating habits is the feeling of being
deprived. With diets our intent is to make rules about certain foods we “can’t” eat. As
you become more aware you realize that there are different parts of the mind and they
don’t always agree.

One part of the mind makes the rule to follow the diet. Another part of the mind reacts
to the rule as if it were being deprived. The characters in our head set up a program of
stories and reactions that then try to influence what we eat and how much. Because not
all parts of the mind have agreed to the rule about what to eat, a conflict in the mind
ensues.

We begin with the authentic desire for our body to be healthy and fit.

However, that desire becomes corrupted by the voices in our head. It turns into a voice
that tells us we can’t or shouldn’t eat something. It is a confining rule that takes away
